passA.summary: Keegan McCallum, founder of the interactive-media inference provider uRun, argues that the interesting frontier in generative video is no longer quality but efficiency and long-horizon, real-time generation. He walks the quality timeline (Will Smith spaghetti → Sora → Sora 2 → SeeDance) only to set it aside, then demos Helios — a real-time distill of Wan 2.1 14B (auto-captioned as 'Juan 2.1') — which produces last-year's-frontier quality continuously and for roughly a hundredth of the cost of minutes-long batch generation. That cost collapse ($10 ≈ 3 hours of continuous video, $50 ≈ 15 hours) unlocks interaction patterns rather than clips: magic-mirror webcam transforms, visual companions for people who don't think in text, and content creation where you steer a generation in under a second instead of pulling a $10-per-minute slot machine. The second half is a pitch: serving this is the hard part (global GPUs, WebRTC/ICE/TURN, multi-model streaming pipelines), so uRun offers a drop-in React component over a programmable Python runtime, plus a CLI and MCP server so agents can build these apps. Worth watching if you care about real-time video infrastructure or interactive AI interfaces; it's eight minutes and mostly a landscape-plus-product talk, not a technical deep dive.
key_points: The quality axis in generative video is largely solved at the frontier, and the underexplored axis is efficiency plus long-horizon continuous generation.
Helios, a real-time distill of Wan 2.1 14B served by uRun, generates clips faster than a viewer can consume them at roughly the quality bar frontier models hit a year earlier.
In a side-by-side, the real-time generation had better motion than the minutes-long batch generation and cost about 1/100th as much.
At least 40 models with real-time and/or long-horizon generation capabilities shipped in the past year, spanning world models, avatar models, and video-to-video transformation.
Economics have crossed a threshold: $10 buys about 3 hours of continuous generated video and $50 buys about 15 hours — a full day of interacting with AI in a visual medium.

Real-time steering replaces the current 'slot machine' content-creation loop of prompts, keyframes, and ~$10 per minute of output, letting creators redirect a generation in under a second and later render a full-fidelity clip with a model like Google Gemini Omni.
Video-native interaction is an accessibility story: it opens the benefits that text-oriented users already get from coding models to people who learn and think visually.

The hard part of building these apps is serving infrastructure — globally distributed GPUs, WebRTC/ICE/TURN, and frame-synchronized multi-model streaming pipelines — which uRun abstracts behind a React component, a Python runtime, a CLI, and an MCP server.

notable_quotes.text: We have the classic Will Smith eating spaghetti from 2023. It is nightmare fuel and not something you would ever mistake for reality.
notable_quotes.why: Sets the quality-timeline baseline the whole talk pivots away from.

notable_quotes.text: I'm here to talk about another axis which models are improving along, which is efficiency and, uh, the long horizon generations.
notable_quotes.why: The talk's thesis in one line.

notable_quotes.text: And the other video, um, is a bunch of clips, um, that have been generated faster than you can consume them.
notable_quotes.why: Defines what 'real-time' concretely means for video generation.

notable_quotes.text: they're about at the same quality as the frontier models were last year
notable_quotes.why: Names the explicit quality tradeoff accepted in exchange for speed.

notable_quotes.text: It's got better motion and it was generated for about a 100th of the cost.
notable_quotes.why: The talk's headline number, and a claim that speed doesn't always cost quality.

notable_quotes.text: There's been at least 40 models with real-time capabilities and long horizon generation capabilities released this year.
notable_quotes.why: Quantifies the pace of the field rather than asserting it vaguely.

notable_quotes.text: And so we're at a place right now where $10 can get you 3 hours worth of generated video continuously with most of these models and $50 would give you an entire day interacting with an AI in a visual medium.
notable_quotes.why: Reframes video cost in terms developers already understand from token spend.

notable_quotes.text: You could ask to see yourself in a car you like or with a haircut you're considering.
notable_quotes.why: Concrete consumer use case for real-time video-to-video.

notable_quotes.text: because these are open-ended models that can transform what they're seeing on a webcam in real time
notable_quotes.why: States the capability that separates these models from fixed-purpose filters.

notable_quotes.text: you know, working with AI involves a lot of reading and a lot of text. For some people that's more difficult.
notable_quotes.why: Frames generative video as an accessibility argument, not just entertainment.

notable_quotes.text: Uh so, there's more opportunities to have companions or visual mediums that are going to allow more people to experience the things a lot of us have with coding models
notable_quotes.why: Ties the visual medium directly to the productivity gains developers already enjoy.

notable_quotes.text: so far we've very much had a slot machine type approach where you're setting up a prompt and maybe some key frames and spending about $10 a minute to try and get the shot that you want
notable_quotes.why: Names the current workflow's failure mode with a price attached.

notable_quotes.text: But with these models you can actually steer them in real time in under a second while they're generating and get the actual shots that you want.
notable_quotes.why: States the proposed replacement for prompt-and-pray generation, with a latency figure.

notable_quotes.text: and with modern models like Google Gemini Omni, you can actually render these out as a more full fidelity clip
notable_quotes.why: Describes the draft-then-render pipeline that reconciles speed with final quality.

notable_quotes.text: You're going to need to set up probably WebRTC and ICE and TURN.
notable_quotes.why: Concretely names the unglamorous infrastructure most teams underestimate.

notable_quotes.text: And for the most interesting use cases, you're going to want a model wire multiple models together in continuous streaming workflows
notable_quotes.why: Argues the interesting applications are multi-model pipelines, not single-model calls.

notable_quotes.text: And so, our idea is what if there was just a React component that you could drop into your application to make it easy to provide video interactively inside your applications with any model.
And I argue that in 2026, don't just need platforms, we need software factories and ways for agents interact with these.
notable_quotes.why: An explicit, contestable claim about how AI infrastructure should be packaged.

notable_quotes.text: And so the models are here and the frontier is really in how we serve them.
notable_quotes.why: The closing argument: the bottleneck has moved from model capability to serving.

positions.claim: The important axis of improvement in generative video is now efficiency and long-horizon generation, not frontier quality.
Real-time generation is not necessarily worse than slow batch generation — the real-time sample had better motion at about 1/100th the cost.
Today's real-time models sit at roughly the quality bar that frontier video models hit one year ago.
At least 40 models with real-time and long-horizon capabilities were released in the past year.
$10 buys about 3 hours of continuous generated video and $50 buys about 15 hours, comparable to what developers already burn on coding tokens.
Current generative video content creation is a slot machine costing about $10 per minute of output, and sub-second real-time steering is the better workflow.
Generative video is an accessibility technology that extends AI's benefits to people who don't think or learn in text.
The discussion of real-time video should not be confined to world models; the more interesting applications are broader.
Building interactive video apps requires globally distributed GPUs, WebRTC/ICE/TURN, and frame-synchronized multi-model pipelines, which is hard enough to justify a hosted abstraction.
In 2026 developers need software factories with CLI and MCP access for agents, not just platforms.
The models are good enough already; the remaining frontier is serving infrastructure.
